s09.slug: TUESDAY · 10:12 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — HIS ROOM
body: At eight Theo stood in the doorway of 412 with the teacup held out in front of him in both hands, at the height of a ring on a pillow, Hollis inside it. “I’m at the house tonight,” he said. “Sigma Rho. I’ll be back at two. Hollis is coming with me.” He took the cup. What he left is its ring on the nightstand, a pale circle in the dust where the egg has spent his retirement.

The front desk at ten past ten is one fluorescent tube and Priya, on duty under a corkboard of flyers for things that have already happened, with the guest log on a clipboard and a pen behind her ear. Skye comes in through the glass doors from the curb with her keys still in her fist and her hair coming down out of its Mass pins, in the gray cardigan, buttoned to the throat. She signs where Jack points. She does *Purpose* fast, with a loop on the end, like she’s signing a headshot.

body.title: Delgado Hall — Guest Log
body.text: Resident: J. Costigan · Room: 412 · Guest: S. Callender · In: 10:12 PM · Purpose: Candlemas

body: Priya reads *Purpose*. Her eyes come up to Skye, and go across to Jack, and whatever she was going to say about the feast of the Presentation she puts back in the drawer. “I’m going to need you to sign out by two.”

He takes Skye’s hand and takes her up the east stairs. He asked her. On the church steps, with the wax gone white on her thumb and the candles still going in the courtyard behind them, he asked her up, and she looked at him and said yes like she was writing it down.

On the landing between three and four, where the light buzzes in its cage and the fire door’s wire window shows an empty hall, he stops and turns her against the rail and tells her what he wants before she can open her mouth. He can do that now — a whole sentence, his eyes on hers, nothing mumbled at the floor: he wants her against his door, and his mouth on her, and he wants her not to make one sound. Skye opens her mouth, and shuts it again, and goes up the last flight ahead of him so fast he has to let go of her hand.

412 is dark except for the parking lot. The sodium lamp out there comes in through the four inches of window he left propped and lays an orange slab across the floor and up the wall, and that is all the light there is. He locks the door behind them, and the bolt is loud. Under the window the radiator clanks as the heat comes on, a sound like somebody dropping a wrench two floors down, and goes quiet.

She has never been here. Every time it has been hers — her car, her room, her bath, her beach — and now she stands in the middle of his floor in her church clothes and takes it in: the narrow bed with the crucifix over it, the porch on Glenwood in a drugstore print with Ma’s thumb in the corner, Theo’s princes, the ring on the nightstand where an egg used to live.

body.text: On his desk, standing in a coffee mug, unlit, is her Candlemas candle, where he put it when they traded.
body.else: On his desk, standing in a coffee mug, unlit, is his Candlemas candle, for Nonna.

body: Rosie’s drawing has slipped on its tack again. Skye puts one finger to the corner and sets it straight. “Who’s the tall one?”
“Me. Rosie did it at Christmas.”
She looks at the crab, which is the size of a dog and smiling. “I’d date the crab,” she says. “Present company —” and he has her by the hips.

He turns her and puts her back to the door, and the door is the only thing separating them from the fourth floor: a slab of painted particleboard, and on the other side of it the hall carpet, Doug’s door, the fire door at the end that bangs every time anybody takes the stairs. Through the wall Doug’s keyboard goes in long patient bursts. Every sound in this building goes everywhere. Jack grew up in a house like that, one bathroom and two sisters and a heating duct that carried everything to Nonna.
He says her name, not loud, and her hand comes down over his mouth before the name is finished. She shakes her head at him, slow. Cinderblock.

So he undresses her without a word. The cardigan first, every button from the throat down, and the white collar under it, and he puts his mouth to each thing he uncovers — the notch of her throat, the top of her breast, the soft place under her arm that makes her jerk against the wood. When her hands come for his shirt he takes them and puts them back on the door beside her hips, and she leaves them there. He kneels on his own floor and takes the rest of her clothes down with him.

She has the heel of her hand jammed against her mouth before he’s even touched her. He puts his mouth on her and she shudders the length of the door. He knows the way by now and goes the long way anyway, slow, unhurried, until her other hand is in his hair and her thighs are shaking against his shoulders and the heel of her hand isn’t enough — a sound starts somewhere in her chest — and he reaches up without stopping and covers her mouth with his own hand, and she bites the side of it.

Out in the hall somebody comes up the stairs. The fire door bangs. Flip-flops, slapping, coming this way, and a girl on a phone: *no, he said that, to her face* — and they freeze, Skye flat to the door with his hand over her mouth and her heartbeat going into the wood, and the flip-flops come past 412 close enough to touch, and keep going, and down the hall a door opens and shuts.

He doesn’t stop for the flip-flops. Maybe that’s what does it. She comes with her teeth in his hand and her knees going, the door taking her weight, shaking from her shoulders down with the work of keeping it in, and the only noise in 412 is the latch, rattling very softly in its plate.

He gets her to the bed. It’s extra-long and narrow as a cot, made this morning by a man who wasn’t expecting this, and he lays her down on it under the crucifix. He knows it’s there. He doesn’t look up at it and he doesn’t pretend it isn’t.

And he makes her wait. Skye Callender doesn’t get made to wait — not by a maître d’, not by a network — and she finds it out by degrees: his hands everywhere but where she wants them, the inside of her elbow, the backs of her knees, the long ladder of her ribs, his mouth following and going slower each time she arches for it. Her eyes say a great deal. She can’t say any of it. Through the wall Doug’s keyboard goes, and stops, and goes. Her hips come up off the mattress and he puts them back down.
She takes his face in both hands, brings it up to hers, and whispers one word against his mouth — *now* — and waits.

He keeps her waiting a little longer. When he gives it to her it’s with his hand between her legs, slow and sure, taking his time, and she comes again with her face turned hard into his shoulder and her teeth in the cotton of his T-shirt.

When she can move she rolls him onto his back and gets his belt open one-handed and takes him in her mouth. He gets his forearm across his own mouth and bites down on it. She is slow about it, slower than he was, like a debt she means to pay with interest, and he lies under the crucifix with his arm across his face and his free hand spread on the cold cinderblock over the bed —
— and the bed frame hits the wall. One flat wooden knock, straight through the block into Doug’s room.
Doug’s keyboard stops.

They freeze. Skye with her mouth off him and her eyes enormous in the orange light, Jack with his arm across his face. Five seconds. Ten. The keyboard starts again. Skye puts her forehead down on his hip and laughs without any sound at all, shaking with it, and that sets him off, and they lie there in a heap shaking with the effort of it until the springs start to creak with them and they have to stop that too.

After that they lie face to face, because the bed has room for nothing else: on their sides, his back to the cinderblock, nothing on either of them now, her leg over his hip and his between hers. They move against each other slowly. They kiss with their mouths open and no sound in it. Every long slide of her along him takes him to the edge she left him at and keeps him there. His hands are open on her back, the fingers spread loose along her spine, and they aren’t keeping anything anywhere. The only thing left is that neither of them has moved the last way, and he can feel how little it would take. It would hardly be a motion.
His mouth is at her ear. On his own bed, under his own crucifix, with the candle on the desk and his brother twenty-three since this morning, he does not know if he would say no tonight.

choices.text: “I don’t know that I’d say no tonight.”
choices.key: In your room, on your bed, you told her you didn’t know that you’d say no tonight. She didn’t ask.
response: He says it into her ear, a whisper, every word of it, and doesn’t take any of it back.
She goes still against him. Her breath stops; her hand on his chest stops; her heel on the back of his calf stops. All he can feel moving in her is her heart, hard, through his own chest.

choices.key: In your room, on your bed, you told her to ask you. She didn’t.
response: Two words, breathed against her ear, and he means them as far as they go.
She goes still. She pulls her head back on the pillow far enough to see his face in the light from the lot, and looks at it, and keeps looking, and her hand comes up and rests along his jaw.

choices.text: *Tell her about the swing — what she told Danny — and hold her.*
choices.key: In your room, on your bed, at the edge, you told her what it was to hear her tell Danny about Montecito, and held her. She didn’t ask.
response: So he tells her that, with his mouth in her hair: that he was about to leave the den too, that night; that he crossed it before he could talk himself out the door; that he didn’t know she kept the book. Then he has nothing left to whisper, and he gets his arms around her and holds her against him, hard.
She pulls back far enough to see him. Whatever is in his face, she looks at it, and hers doesn’t hide what it does to her.

choices.text: *Say the no before she has to choose.*
choices.key: In your room, on your bed, at the edge, you said no before she had to choose. She wasn’t going to ask.
response: “Not tonight,” he whispers, before anything else can get said, before she has to choose a thing.
Against his throat Skye starts to laugh without a sound, her mouth open on his skin, shaking.

s09a.slug: TUESDAY · 11:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — TO THE LETTER

body.text: “No,” she whispers. “You don’t get to hand it to me like that.”
“I know,” she whispers. “I could tell. That’s why I’m not going to.”
“I know what you’re not saying,” she whispers. “I’m not going to make you say it.”
“I wasn’t going to ask,” she whispers. “You beat me to it. Don’t get used to that.”

body: She comes up on an elbow so her mouth is at his ear, and gives him her reasons fast and low, counting them off on his chest with one finger, the way she runs down a script she’s passing on.

“One. Not in this bed. Not the first time. It’s an ironing board with a crucifix over it, and your sister drew that crab, and the crab would *know*.” Her breath is hot and quick against his ear. “Two. It’s your brother’s birthday. I talked to him this afternoon. I told him to call us. I’m not doing it on Danny’s birthday.”
The finger stops on his breastbone.

“Three.” The speed goes out of it. “Tomorrow night you walk into that little room at eight o’clock and tell him you won’t, and I want you to be able to mean it when you say it. I’m not going to be the thing that makes you a liar in there.”
She puts her forehead against his temple.
“When I ask again,” she whispers, “I want you to have nowhere to be in the morning.”

body.text: The only no in the room is his, said early, to a question nobody put. Nothing has been asked.
body.else: Nothing has been refused. Nothing has been asked.

body: He lies there with his hands open on her back and the whole of it in them, and he takes a breath to say something, and holds it. She feels him take it. She puts her mouth over his before he can decide what it was for.
So the line stays where it was, and everything else goes on up against it, at the same heat, without a sound.

They bring each other the rest of the way together this time — on their sides under the window, her hand closed around him and his between her legs, their mouths sealed over each other’s to keep it in. It takes a long time. She finds his rhythm and he finds hers and for a while they only match, breath for breath, into each other’s mouths, both of them shaking with the work of keeping still everywhere but there. When it comes it comes for both of them inside the same few seconds, her cry and his going into each other’s mouths and nowhere else, his hips jerking against her hand, her thighs clamping down on his, the bed holding perfectly, miraculously quiet. Afterward they stay like that, mouths together, breathing, wet and sweating in a room with the heat on, and he can feel her heart slowing down against him a beat at a time.

They don’t sleep. She traces the scar through his eyebrow with her thumb, and he traces the horse she drew on his ribs on Monday morning, faded now to a gray ghost of a horse, and through the wall Doug logs off with a sigh you can hear through cinderblock.
The radiator knocks at one.

It goes off under the window like a hammer on a pipe, and the two of them come up off the mattress the way you come up when a cruiser’s lights go on behind you — Skye halfway to sitting with the sheet clutched to her chest, Jack’s heart going like Ma just opened the door. Their eyes go to the radiator. She falls back down onto his chest and shakes, and he puts his face into her hair to keep his own laughing in, and the bed gives one long warning creak, and they freeze all over again, and that’s worse.

s09b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:05 AM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE QUESTION UNDER THE CRUCIFIX
body: After that, the streetlight. The lamp in the parking lot has the room to itself: the orange slab up the wall and across the bed and over the two of them, and the crucifix above them turned dark copper. His arm is under her neck and has been asleep for some time, and he doesn’t move it.
Skye lies on his chest with her chin on her hands and looks up at the crucifix — the small bronze body, the wood behind it, the lamp on both. She looks at it for some time and doesn’t make a joke.

Then she does Danny’s laugh into his chest. Badly. A wheeze with a motor in it, the air going out of him in pieces, and Jack has to pull the pillow over both their heads, and from under it, muffled: “Sorry, sir. Family news.”
When the pillow comes off she’s smiling. She puts her chin back on her hands.
“He called me Mary Catherine,” she says.
“Gina.”

“Gina,” she agrees. “Gina’s a wire service.” She thinks about it. “My mother doesn’t even call me that. She says *Skye* on the phone when it’s only us, in case somebody’s listening. Your brother’s on a recorded line in a prison, and he said it anyway.”

“Good evening, Central Coast,” she says, low, in a weather girl’s bright shut-in voice, “and here’s your extended forecast. Tomorrow: Hale, partly cloudy. The weekend: Saints, with a chance of — ” and stops, and puts her hand over his heart instead of finishing it.
“Is there a version of later I’m in,” she says. “If I never believe it.”
He starts to answer and she puts a finger on his lip.
“Not the logic. I have the logic. I’ve read the section. I read it on my phone in the makeup chair. I know I’m technically on your books.” Her finger doesn’t move. “The *thing*.”
She turns her head and lays her cheek on his chest, facing the window.

“My father married my mother in a church,” she says. “St. Mary’s, in Lancaster. Pat Doyle. He had a rented suit for it — there’s one picture she didn’t cut him out of. He was gone by the time I was four.” The lamp buzzes outside, faint. “So I don’t think the church part is what keeps anybody. I know that’s not an argument. I know you could take it apart in your sleep. It’s just the only wedding I’ve got.”
He doesn’t take it apart. He puts his hand in her hair and leaves it there.
Down in the lot a car door shuts, and somebody’s keys, and then nothing anywhere on four.

She lifts her head to say the rest. “I watched you kneel tonight,” she says. “Everybody went up and you stayed down, and I held your candle. I’d hold it every Sunday. I would. I liked holding it.” “But I can’t go up with you. Not if I don’t believe it. That’s the one thing I won’t fake, Jack. Not for anybody. Not for you, especially.” “So is there a later where that’s allowed to be fine?”
Her ear has gone back down over his heart. Whatever it’s doing, she’s listening to it do it.

choices.key: Under the crucifix Skye asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. You told her what Nonna said: Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife.
response: “Sunday night,” he says. “After you fell asleep on me. Gina texted, one in the morning, Nonna had woken her up to send it.” He tells her the rest: Nonna says *Maria Caterina* is a good name for a wife.
Skye goes very still on his chest. He feels it go through her and stop. “Your grandmother’s never met me.”
“She’s lit two candles.”

She’s quiet so long he hears the elevator go down to the lobby and come back up empty. When she speaks it’s with a little lift in it, a girl being fine: “Tell her it’s a good name for a lot of things.” And then, with her face turned down into his neck where he can’t see it, with no lift in it at all: “Tell her thank you.”

choices.key: Under the crucifix Skye asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. You told her she’s in all of it.
response: “All of it,” she says. She turns it over. “That’s a big part.”
“You’re a big actress.”
She smiles; he can feel it on his chest. When it goes she lifts her head. “Don’t give me all of it if you don’t have it, Jack.”

“I have it.” And because she’ll want the specifics, he gives her some: Sunday Mass with her beside him. Glenwood at Christmas, Nonna feeding her till she can’t stand up and then feeding her standing. Danny on the phone asking for her first. “All of it,” he says. “I wasn’t rounding.”
She looks at him. She puts her head back down over his heart and lets him have said it.

choices.text: “I don’t know how it works yet. I want it to.”
choices.key: Under the crucifix Skye asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. You told her you don’t know how it works yet, and you want it to.
response: “I know what the Church says about it,” he says. “I could cite you the canon. I don’t know what it looks like in a kitchen on a Tuesday. I want to find out.”
“That is a very Catholic sentence,” she says. “*Wanting it to.*”
Her fingernail starts on his ribs, over what’s left of Monday’s horse, going around and around the same line.
“Find out,” she says into his chest. “I’ll wait. I’m bad at waiting.” The fingernail stops. “I’ll do it anyway.”

s09c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:45 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH FLOOR → THE LOBBY
body: They dress in the orange light with their backs half turned, which is ridiculous after everything, and she says so, and does it anyway. The white collar. The gray cardigan, buttoned wrong, and undone, and buttoned right. Her hair twisted up off her neck and stuck through with a pen from his desk.

body.text: On her way to the door she passes the desk and her candle standing in its mug in the streetlight, and touches the wick with one finger as she goes by.
body.else: On her way to the door she passes the desk and his candle standing in its mug in the streetlight, Nonna’s, and touches the wick with one finger as she goes by.

body: He walks her down. The fourth-floor hall at a quarter to two is brown carpet and shut doors and the exit sign humming red at the far end, and halfway along it, where the hall opens out, the lounge is lit.

Theo is in it. So is Laney, cross-legged on the couch in a Pi Lam sweatshirt with a yellow highlighter crosswise in her teeth. So is Margot at the long table, a notebook open in front of her and the pen held over it, uncapped. So is Kevin, in plaid pajama pants and a hooded sweatshirt, with his arms folded so tight it looks structural. And the whiteboard on its rolling stand, which Theo, as Jack and Skye come level with the doorway, puts a hand to and sends spinning on its pivot so hard it keeps going — blank side, writing side, blank side. On the way around Jack gets a column of names in three colors of marker, and under it a car: four wheels, and inside it six circles.
Everybody in the lounge holds still. The whiteboard doesn’t.
“Book club,” Theo says.
“*Dubliners*,” says Margot.
“Hi, guys!” says Kevin, sunny and in pain. “I’m here under protest. Margot’s here for science.”
Laney takes the highlighter out of her teeth long enough to say “Evenin’,” to Skye, in a voice like a frost advisory for the Panhandle, and puts it back.
The whiteboard comes to rest blank side out and rocks a little on its casters.
At the stairwell door Skye looks back over her shoulder at the lit doorway, mild as milk. “Somebody’s running lines,” she says. “Big cast.” And she takes the stairs.

In the lobby Priya is asleep over the guest log with her cheek on her forearm and the pen still in her fingers. Skye slides the clipboard out from under her elbow without waking her and signs herself out — *Out: 1:52* — and then, next to *Purpose*, writes something more, small and quick, and slides the clipboard back under Priya’s arm before he can lean over and read it.

The Saab is at the curb with the top up and the windows fogged from the inside. He gets in the passenger side to say goodnight with the doors shut, and she kisses him across the gearshift with the engine running and her hand fisted in the front of his T-shirt, long and slow, the gearshift digging into his ribs in a way he’ll feel tomorrow. When he gets out she leans across the passenger seat to the open window and looks up at him.

body.text: “All of it,” she says, and goes.

body: He takes the east stairs back up. On four the lounge is still lit, and as he comes past, the door is swinging shut on its arm, and through the last of the gap comes Laney’s voice, low and fast and urgent — “— she’d *decided*, Theo —” — and the door closes on it.

In 412 he gets into bed in his T-shirt. The pillow smells like her shampoo and the room smells like the radiator. The crucifix is a dark shape on the wall over him, and the lamp in the lot hums, and his hand, where she bit it, is sore.

Theo comes in at 2:20 without turning on the light. He says nothing. Jack hears his shoes come off, one and then the other, and the springs of the other bed, and last, very carefully, the teacup set back down on the nightstand in its own ring.
